'''Gino Claudio Segrè''' (born October 4, 1938) is an Italian-American physicist and professor [[emeritus]] at the [[University of Pennsylvania]].  He is the author of several books on the history of science, particularly on atomic physics. Segrè's ''Faust in Copenhagen'' was a finalist in the [[Los Angeles Times Book Fair]]<ref name=latimes>{{cite news |url=http://events.latimes.com/bookprizes/previous-winners/year-2007/ |title=2007 Los Angeles Times Book Prizes Winners |work=[[Los Angeles Times]] |date=11 April 2007 |access-date=2014-08-19 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130424170625/http://events.latimes.com/bookprizes/previous-winners/year-2007/ |archive-date=24 April 2013 }}</ref> and winner of the [[American Institute of Physics]] [[Science Writing Award]].<ref name=aip>{{cite press release| url=http://www.newswise.com/articles/american-institute-of-physics-announces-awards-for-best-science-writing1 |title=American Institute of Physics Announces Awards for Best Science Writing |publisher=American Institute of Physics| date=24 February 2009| access-date=2014-08-19}}</ref>

==Birth and education==
Gino Segrè was born in [[Florence]], Italy, to an [[Italian Jew]]ish father (Angelo Segrè) and a [[German Catholic]] mother (Katherine "Katia" {{nee|Schall}}). Following [[Italian racial laws|the anti-semitic laws enacted in Italy]] in 1938, family immigrated to [[New York City]] in May 1939, where they resided for 8 years before returning to Florence.<ref name=penn>{{cite journal| url=https://thepenngazette.com/old-friends/ |title=Old Friends| journal=Penn Gazette |date=November–December 2011| access-date=2014-08-19}}</ref> Segrè's uncle, Nobel laureate physicist [[Emilio Segrè]], also emigrated to the United States for the same reason.

Gino Segrè received a Bachelor of Arts degree from [[Harvard College]] in 1959 and a Ph.D. degree in physics from [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] in 1963. Afterwards, Segrè became a fellow at [[CERN]] and the [[University of California, Berkeley]].  He joined the University of Pennsylvania department of physics as a professor in 1967, where he remained until he retired in 2007.  His honors include fellowships from [[John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation|Guggenheim Foundation]], [[Sloan Foundation]] and [[Rockefeller Foundation]].

==Books==
Since 2002, Segrè has published four books on the [[history of science]].

''The Pope of Physics: Enrico Fermi and the Birth of the Atomic Age'' was published in 2016.<ref>{{cite book|title=The Pope of Physics: Enrico Fermi and the Birth of the Atomic Age|publisher=Henry Holt and Company|url=|isbn=978-1-627-79005-5|last1=Segrè |first1=Gino |last2=Hoerlin |first2=Bettina |date= |year=2016|location=New York}}</ref> Written with his wife Bettina Hoerlin,<ref>{{cite news|title=Penn husband-and-wife team pen biography on 'Pope of Physics' |newspaper=Penn Today|author=Sundermeier, Ali|date=December 22, 2016|url=https://penntoday.upenn.edu/news/penn-husband-and-wife-team-pen-biography-on-pope-of-physics}}</ref> ''The Pope of Physics''<ref>{{cite book|last1=Segre|first1=Gino|last2=Hoerlin|first2=Bettina|title=The Pope of Physics: Enrico Fermi and the Birth of the Atomic Age|publisher=[[Henry Holt and Company]]|isbn=978-1-62779-005-5|postscript=; hbk 1st edition, 368 pp.|date=2016-10-18}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1063/PT.3.3401| title=Review of ''The Pope of Physics: Enrico Fermi and the Birth of the Atomic Age'' | year=2016 | last1=Westfall | first1=Catherine | author-link=Catherine Westfall | journal=Physics Today | volume=69 | issue=12 | pages=57–58 | bibcode=2016PhT....69l..57W | doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.5406/italamerrevi.7.2.0217| title=Review of ''The Pope of Physics: Enrico Fermi and the Birth of the Atomic Age'' | year=2017 | last1=Turchetti | first1=Simone | journal=Italian American Review | volume=7 | issue=2 | pages=217–219 | s2cid=246623847 | doi-access=free }}</ref> explores the life and career of famous Italian physicist [[Enrico Fermi]], whose colleagues referred to him as the Pope due to his infallibility.<ref>{{cite journal|author=Cifarelli, Luisa|author-link=Luisa Cifarelli|title=Review of ''The Pope of Physics: Enrico Fermi and the Birth of the Atomic Age'' by Gino Segrè and Bettina Hoerlin|journal=CERN Courier|year=2018|url=https://cds.cern.ch/record/2654726/files/vol58-issue10-p049-e.pdf}}</ref>  Fermi has a rich legacy of scientific advances, and is best known for his leadership in building the atomic bomb. "Pope of Physics" was reviewed by ''[[The Wall Street Journal]]''<ref>{{cite news|last1=Crumey|first1=Andrew|title=Father of the Atomic Age|url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/father-of-the-atomic-age-1477074176|access-date=5 March 2017}}</ref> and ''[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]''.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Farmelo|first1=Graham|title=Physics: Fallible pontiff of physics|journal=Nature|date=13 October 2016|volume=538|issue=7624|pages=168–169|doi=10.1038/538168a|bibcode=2016Natur.538..168F|s2cid=4386300|doi-access=free}}</ref>

Segrè's 2011 book ''Ordinary Geniuses'' is a dual biography of [[Max Delbruck]] and [[George Gamow]], two physicists who made major contributions to the field of biology with their "pioneering" spirits and practical jokes.<ref name=ordinary>{{cite book| last=Segrè| first=Gino| title=Ordinary Geniuses: Max Delbruck, George Gamow and the Origins of Genomics and Big-Bang Cosmology| date=18 August 2011| publisher=Viking-Penguin| isbn=978-0-670-02276-2| url-access=registration| url=https://archive.org/details/ordinarygeniuses00gino}}</ref> ''Ordinary Geniuses'' was reviewed by [[Jeremy Bernstein]] in ''The Wall Street Journal''<ref name="bernstein">{{cite news |last=Bernstein |first=Jeremy |url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/SB10001424053111904888304576472690333523916 |title=Book Review: ''Ordinary Geniuses'' |work=Wall Street Journal |date=13 August 2011 |access-date=2014-08-19 |url-access=subscription }}</ref> and [[Jonathon Keats]] in ''[[New Scientist]]''.<ref name="keats">{{cite web |last=Keats |first=Jonathon |url=https://www.newscientist.com/blogs/culturelab/2011/08/a-pair-of-maverick-physicists.html |title=CultureLab: A pair of maverick physicists |publisher= |date=24 August 2011 |access-date=2014-08-19|website=The New Scientist}}</ref>

Segrè's 2007 book ''Faust in Copenhagen'' recounts how a group of 40 physicists assembled at [[Copenhagen Institute|Niels Bohr's Copenhagen Institute]] focusing on the [[discovery of the neutron]].<ref name=faust>{{cite book| last=Segrè| first=Gino| title=Faust in Copenhagen: A Struggle for the Soul of Physics| url=https://archive.org/details/faustincopenhage00segr| url-access=registration| year=2007| publisher=Viking| isbn=978-0-14-311373-7}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1063/1.2897952| title=review of 2 books: ''Faust in Copenhagen: A Struggle for the Soul of Physics'' by Gino Segrè; ''The Mental Aftermath: The Mentality of German Physicists, 1945—1949'' by Klaus Hentschel (translated from German by Ann M. Hentschel) | year=2008 | last1=Walker | first1=Mark | journal=Physics Today | volume=61 | issue=3 | pages=53–54 }}</ref>  On the final night of the meeting, the younger physicists mount a skit that was a parody of [[Faust|Goethe's Faust]], adapted to the world of physics.  By Segrè's description, "What the physicists didn't realize was that within a year, [[Adolf Hitler's rise to power|Hitler's ascent to power]] would change their world and within a decade their studies of the atomic nucleus would force them to make their own Faustian bargains." ''Faust in Copenhagen'' was reviewed in the ''Sunday [[The New York Times|New York Times]]'' book section by [[George Johnson (writer)|George Johnson]].<ref name=johnson>{{cite news| last=Johnson| first=George| url=https://www.nytimes.com/2007/06/24/books/review/Johnson-t.html|title=Meta Physicists| newspaper=The New York Times| date=24 June 2007| access-date=2014-08-19}}</ref>

Segrè's 2002 book ''A Matter of Degrees: What Temperature Reveals about the Past and Future of our Species, Planet and Universe''<ref>{{cite book| last=Segrè| first=Gino| title=A Matter of Degrees: What Temperature Reveals about the Past and Future of our Species, Planet and Universe| year=2002| publisher=Viking| isbn=978-0-14-200278-0}}</ref> explores [[temperature]]'s many mysteries, from the causes of fevers in humans to the [[origin of the universe]]. [[Marcia Bartusiak]] reviewed ''Matter of Degrees'' in ''The New York Times''.<ref>{{cite news| first=Marcia |last=Bartusiak |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2002/08/04/books/fahrenheit-451000.html |title=Fahrenheit 451,000| work=[[The New York Times]] |date=4 August 2002| access-date=2014-08-19}}</ref>

==Scientific research==
Segrè's research covers [[high-energy physics]], including grand unification and the [[fine-structure constant]],<ref>{{cite journal|title=Implications of gauge unification for time variation of the fine structure constant  |date=February 2002 |doi=10.1016/S0370-2693(02)01189-9 |volume=528 |issue=1–2  |journal=Physics Letters B |pages=121–128|arxiv=hep-ph/0112233 |bibcode=2002PhLB..528..121L |last1=Langacker  |first1=Paul  |last2=Segrè  |first2=Gino  |last3=Strassler  |first3=Matthew J  |s2cid=8773425 |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0370269302011899|author-link3=Matthew Strassler}}</ref> and [[astrophysics]], including [[baryon asymmetry]], [[pulsar kick]]s,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Kusenko |first=Alexander |author-link=Alexander Kusenko |last2=Segrè |first2=Gino |date=February 1999 |title=Pulsar kicks from neutrino oscillations |url=https://journals.aps.org/prd/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevD.59.061302 |journal=Physical Review D |volume=59 |issue=6 |article-number=061302 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevD.59.061302|arxiv=astro-ph/9811144 }}</ref> and neutrino oscillations.<ref>{{Cite journal| arxiv=hep-ph/9606428 |title=Velocities of pulsars and neutrino oscillations |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=77 |issue=24 |pages=4872–4875 |date=1996 |last1=Kusenko |first1=Alexander |last2=Segrè |first2=Gino |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.77.4872 |pmid=10062656 |bibcode=1996PhRvL..77.4872K |s2cid=14679410 |url=https://journals.aps.org/prl/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevLett.77.4872}}</ref>

==Personal life==
Segrè is married to Bettina Hoerlin (born 1939), a former [[Philadelphia]] Health Commissioner.  She is the daughter of [[Los Alamos, New Mexico|Los Alamos]] physicist Hermann Hoerlin and Kate (née Tietz, formerly Schmid). Hoerlin has chronicled her parents meeting and departure from [[Nazi Germany]] in her book ''Steps of Courage''.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://bettinahoerlin.com |title=Steps of Courage: My Parents' Journey from Nazi Germany to America |publisher=Bettinahoerlin.com |date= |access-date=2014-08-19 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141111172607/http://bettinahoerlin.com/ |archive-date=2014-11-11 }}</ref>  Together they have seven children (including [[Julie Segre]] and [[Kristine Yaffe]]) and nine grandchildren. They live in Philadelphia.
